name: aida_r5_dining_drill_screw
purpose: The drill used as a drill: the R5 picks it up by its pistol grip (as aida_r5_dining_drill), brings its bit onto a #8 wood screw started in a plywood board standing on the table, pulls the trigger in the drill's low gear and feeds the drill behind the screw as it goes in, until its head seats - rung 4 of the power drill's use ladder (a bit in the chuck pressed into a workpiece: a screw driven).

fixtures.name: Board
fixtures.why: an 18 mm birch-plywood board standing on the dining table, its face square to the drill's spindle as the lift leaves it; static (clamped). Built round a 9 mm square hole at the screw - its pilot hole and countersink: a solid board stopped the bit's tip at its face, the recess's lower half inside the board's volume, and the screw could not seat (0.5 mm short, 2026-10-16)

fixtures.name: Screw
fixtures.why: a #8 x 1-1/4 in flat-head square-drive wood screw (4.17 mm major diameter, head ~8.2 mm, 15 TPI), started 5 mm into a pilot hole; its head built round a 2.8 mm square recess (a #2 square drive) that captures the bit's tip - a flat head let the pressed tip skate off the axis and the screw stopped (2026-10-16); kinematic: behaviors.screw_drive moves it

screw_drive.why: planned live after the lift (screw_then.py): the bit's tip where the drill sits in the hand then, brought onto the screw's axis 15 mm off its head, pressed 1 mm onto it, the trigger pulled (low gear: 450 rpm at full travel), the hand fed along the axis at 0.8 of the screw's own advance (the screw turns only with the bit in its head, so it follows the hand), held a second while the clutch slips at the seat, the trigger let go, the bit drawn back 3 cm

sources.drill: DeWalt DCD771 (18 V compact drill/driver): no-load 0-450 / 0-1500 rpm, max torque 24 N m soft / 42 N m hard - https://service.dewalt.co.uk/BD/IE/en-IE/Product/ProductDetail?id=33336 ; the asset's motor law already runs at 1500 rpm full travel (its high gear)
sources.screw: #8 wood screw: 15 threads per inch, coarse, single lead; major diameter 0.157-0.168 in (ASME B18.6.1 per supplier datasheets) - https://cdefasteners.com/product/47066 , https://www.zoro.com/zoro-select-wood-screw-no-8-3-in-zinc-plated-steel-flat-head-square-drive-100-pk-u251400160300/i/G2566523/
sources.torques: Kumpenza et al. 2020, Engineering Reports, doi:10.1002/eng2.12211: 4.8 mm wood screws into birch plywood (680 kg/m3, 3.5 mm pilot) went in at a driving torque of ~1 N m; tightened to 3, 4 and 5 N m for 12, 16 and 20 mm joints

screw_drive.spin_up_why: the index pulls the trigger at its motor's pace (the drill take's pull took ~2 s of plan for 1.6 rad); the feed waits 0.6 s for the chuck to turn, or the bit would be fed into a head it is not yet turning
screw_drive.throttle_why: the index stalls the trigger at 31-38 % of its travel (every drill take: the Ability Hand's fingertip force against the trigger's spring), so the chuck turns ~150 of its 450 rpm and the feed is sized for that - fed for full speed it outran the screw 2.4x
screw_drive.preload_why: the tip sent 1.5 mm down into the 2.6 mm recess (free space now: no face to press - 3 mm into a flat head pushed the drill back through the grip, 2026-10-16)
screw_drive.resqueeze_why: the trigger re-squeezed every second: the index, halted on it at the post-contact voltage, stayed at 1.287 rad while the drill crept 2 mm in the grip and the trigger let go (34 % to 0, the screw stopped at 11.8 of 26.8 mm, 2026-10-16); 1.15 rad is just below where it stalls, a reversal that clears the halt (ability_hand_model), and the close after drives it on at full voltage
screw_drive.feed_fraction_why: the hand fed at half the screw's rate at the trigger's stalled speed, so the screw waits for the hand and never the hand for the screw: at 0.8 a dip in speed let the arm outrun it, the tip bottomed in the recess and pushed the drill back through the grip, the index (held in the hand) let the trigger forward by as much as the drill slid, and the screw slowed further (5.3 mm slide, 2026-10-16)
screw_drive.over_why: fed 8 mm past the seat: the drill creeps back ~7 mm in the grip over a drive (the index re-squeezing the trigger pulls it toward the heel of the palm), so the bit advances that much less than the hand - the screw stopped 1.2 mm short of its seat (2026-10-16); fed past it, the clutch slips at the seated head
screw_drive.seat_why: held still 0.8 s, the trigger pulled, while the clutch slips at the seated head: leaning on in the seat (tried) only pushed a tip already bottomed in the recess and shoved the drill 2.3 mm back in the grip - the 0.5 mm the screw stopped short of its seat was the board, solid where its countersink should be
screw_drive.index_release_why: the index back only to where it meets the trigger (the tool plan's touch, 1.06 rad), staying on it: let go to 0.98 after a drive had crept the drill 11 mm in the grip, the drill turned down in the hand by 14 mm more as the bit was drawn back (2026-10-16)

objects.name: Drill
objects.label: the cordless drill

physics.collision_overrides_why: the drill body's convex decomposition (16 hulls, PhysX default) covers 25 of the trigger's 46 vertices and the face the finger presses: every rig pull stalled on the body's hull in front of the trigger. An SDF (256: 0.7 mm cells over 18 cm) is the body's own surface; the robot's casing already collides through one in these CPU-physics scenes

objects.why: drill_1: the library's articulated power drill (chuck, clutch, trigger, forward/reverse switch, press-fit battery, the motor law in simReady:behaviors), reprocessed 2026-10-15 so its links carry the class's mass (1.46 kg). 18 cm long and 18.5 cm tall, a compact drill's size (drill_65b826 is the same model at 31 cm). Turned -90 deg: its chuck (asset -x) points along world +y, away from the robot; standing on its battery, the handle 4.7 cm behind the footprint's centre, 9 cm in from the table's edge

attachments.name: Bit
attachments.why: a 50 mm #2 square-drive power bit's 1/4 in hex shank in the chuck, 5 mm in the jaws

attachments.name: BitTip
attachments.why: the bit's square tip, 9 mm beyond the shank, modelled round and thin (1.6 mm) in the recess's 2.8 mm: the recess's taper that centres a real bit is not modelled, and the play takes the 0.4 mm the arm lands within after its looks

tool_grip.why: the pistol grip of a left hand: the palm on the handle's left side (the tool's left: up x forward), the fingers pointing forward and wrapping the handle's front, the index uppermost at the trigger's height, the thumb round the back; the hand's frame from the tool's own parts (the motor behaviour's throttle joint is the trigger, its body the handle's body, the output joint's axis the spindle) - nothing hand-placed
tool_grip.thumb_why: the thumb clear of the tool, out of the grip: the search's only thumb that met the tool closed on the barrel's TOP and pressed the drill down with 13-17 N, a load the fingers then held as well as its weight (drill take 3, 2026-10-15); no thumb rotation wraps the handle without striking it first
tool_grip.settle_shifts_why: seated at the heel the drill no longer sags down the handle (0.3 mm on the rig) but sits 1 cm deeper toward the wrist than the seat predicts (rig, 2026-10-15); the index must meet the trigger first, with room to pull, there too
tool_grip.along_why: 1 mm steps up the handle: the index must lie within the trigger's height and the middle below its bottom edge, and the gap between the two fingers is 4 mm - the trigger's bottom edge has to land in it
tool_grip.finger_edge_why: the index may overhang the trigger's bottom edge by up to 6 mm: with the body's exact (SDF) surface there is open space in front of the handle under the trigger (the 'stall on the body below the trigger' was the convex decomposition's bloat); the middle must stay off the trigger and its travel - it pre-pulled it 2.9 mm and blocked it at 3.3 mm (SDF rig)
tool_grip.force_score_why: the index's modelled force does not rank this drill's grips: it is computed where the grip puts the drill, and the drill settles 1-2.5 cm and 4-7 deg in the hand before the pull. Ranked by it, the planner chose a grip that pulled the trigger 15% (take 7) against the 50% of the grip the old ranking chose (take 4); the knuckle grips it favours pulled 54-68% (takes 5-6, 2026-10-15). The model gates nothing here until it predicts the settle (backlog)
tool_grip.incumbent_why: the best grip the critic loop has measured on this drill (take 4, 2026-10-15: trigger 50%, three grip features failed - thumb_opposes, full_trigger_travel, seats_as_planned). Tried: knuckle pull (takes 5-6: 68% with the middle on the trigger, 54% with the drill sliding 2.5 cm), the force-ranked grip (take 7: 15%). Replace it when a take fails fewer features
tool_grip.trigger_why: the main plan only takes the drill up: the drive (screw_drive) pulls the trigger, planned live against where the drill settled in the hand

grasp_plan.why: reach a staging pose 7 cm to the handle's left with the hand open (the thumb laid flat), slide in to 3 mm from the handle, close the middle, ring, pinky and thumb (the grip command) with the index stopped just short of the trigger, lift 8 cm on the shoulder slide (HomeHero's lift rule), pull the trigger, run 2 s, let it go, hold

hand_model.why: halt-on-collision (ICD word 007) set near the full supply, as for the scissors: the position loop governs, each digit squeezes until it stalls at full voltage and its worm then holds it. A power grip on a 1.46 kg tool wants that squeeze, and the index must push into the trigger's spring (1500 N/m, 15 N at full travel) - at the 3 V default it halted on first touching the trigger. One threshold for the whole hand, as on the real hand. Post-contact (word 008) at 2 V, the top of the ICD's range: with 0 V the squeeze stored at the halt drained out of the pads as the 1.46 kg drill sagged in the hand during the lift and it slid out (drill take 3); a current after contact keeps the digits closing in as the load moves, as the can and the towel use; the worm still holds every digit against its load

tool.why: the drill's motor law (behaviors.motor) run on its joints each control tick: the trigger's travel and the switch give the chuck's target speed (forward, 1500 rpm at full travel); the chuck's drive a velocity drive (no spring), damping 0.05 per degree, 5 N m - the asset's 0.001 is a free spindle's, not a motor's
tool.behavior_overrides_why: the DCD771's low gear (0-450 rpm), the one a screw is driven in; the asset's 1500 rpm is its high gear
tool.drive_max_force_why: the clutch: set where the screw seats and the clutch then slips (1.2 N m: above the ~1 N m the thread takes to form, below the 3-5 N m a joint is tightened to) - at 1.5 N m the stalled motor's reaction kicked the drill back in the thumbless grip as the head seated; the drill's own 24/42 N m would strip it; DeWalt does not publish the clutch's torque per position

grasp_replay.live_plan_why: the drill settles on its battery after the build drops it 2 mm; the grip is planned against where it then stands
grasp_replay.why: the drill's tool grip (plan_er_grasp.py, task tool_grip, tool_grip_planner.py)

screw.why: behaviors.screw_drive every physics step: the wood takes ~1 N m while the thread forms (Kumpenza 2020), 4 N m tightened a quarter turn past seating (their 16 mm joint), stripping at 6 N m (~1.5x: their tightening torque is midway between seating and stripping); the bit drives the screw while its tip is down in the recess (0.5 mm or more below the head's top, within 0.8 mm of the axis, 8 deg of its line) - risen out of it, the screw stops until the hand brings it back down
screw.engage_lateral_why: anywhere the tip can be while down in the recess: the square's half-diagonal (1.98 mm) less the tip's radius (0.8 mm) - 0.8 mm (the square's half-width less the tip's) read a tip sitting in a corner of the turning recess as out of it, the screw paused while the arm fed on, the tip bottomed and pushed the drill back through the grip (2026-10-16)

grasp_replay.then_why: look, correct, spin, look, drive: each stage planned live from where the bit IS after the one before. The arm carrying the drill landed 10 mm off the screw's axis and 4.4 mm short (a second look brought it to 0.3 mm); pulling the trigger with the bit on the head shifted the drill 11.8 mm in the hand - so the trigger is pulled at the 15 mm standoff, the shift corrected with the trigger held, and the bit meets the screw already turning (takes 2026-10-16)

film.why: the close-up on the grip and the lift, then from the side on the bit and the screw for the drive

extra_cameras.name: GraspCloseup
extra_cameras.why: aimed by line of sight (scripts/film_camera.py on the passing rig's log: the robot's links posed from the logged joints, sight lines to the index tip, the palm and the drill body over 76 ticks of the close, lift, pull and release): from the drill's right side, 45 cm out, 30 deg toward its front, 15 deg up - where the fingertips wrap the handle's front and the index sits on the trigger; every sight line clear

extra_cameras.name: ScrewSide
extra_cameras.why: square to the bit's axis at the screw's height, from the drill's free side (the hand holds it from the other): the bit's tip on the screw's head, the screw turning into the board edge-on
